**Case 3: podcast promotion, revisited.** Back to `podcast_promo.csv` from coding block 1.

1.  Draw the scatter plot of downloads against promotion spend again, now with **both axes logged**. What has changed?
2.  Fit the **log-log model** of downloads on promotion spend and host followers. Interpret both coefficients as **elasticities**: what does a 10% increase in spend do to downloads?
3.  Compare the **R²** of the log-log model with the linear model from block 1. Which model would you use to advise the network on its promotion budget?

**Case 4: winning back users.** 1,200 users who uninstalled the app received a win-back offer with a **randomly assigned discount** of 0% to 60%. The data set `app_reinstall.csv` records the discount (`discount`), the user's sessions in the month before uninstalling (`prior_use`), and whether the user **reinstalled** the app within 30 days (`reinstalled`, 1/0).

1.  Compute the **share of reinstalls per discount level** and plot it against the discount. Describe the shape.
2.  Fit a **logistic regression** of `reinstalled` on `discount` and `prior_use`. Interpret the sign and the **odds ratio** of the discount.
3.  Predict the reinstall probability for a user with 10 prior sessions at a discount of **10%, 11%, 40%, and 41%**. By how many percentage points does one more point of discount change the probability in each case — and why do the two answers differ?

The solutions will be available after the session.
:::

## What observational data can and cannot tell you {#sec-obs-limits}

This chapter equipped you with two strategies for causal questions without randomization, and with a tool that is useful regardless of causality. (For a deeper, still readable treatment of these strategies, @angrist2009 remains the standard reference.)

- **Adjustment** (@sec-obs-adjust) handles confounders you can **measure**. It is only as good as your variables: with a perfect proxy for the confounder, it recovers the truth; with no proxy, it changes nothing. The assumption behind it — **exogeneity**, the treatment is uncorrelated with everything left in the error term — can never be tested in the data; it has to be argued from theory and from how the data came to be.
- **Difference-in-differences** (@sec-obs-did) handles confounders that are **constant over time**, measured or not — but it requires parallel trends, which the pre-period can make plausible but never prove.
- **Prediction** (@sec-obs-prediction) needs no causal assumptions at all. A regression that predicts well is valuable even if none of its coefficients can be interpreted as an effect.

Whichever strategy you use, report it the way @sec-experiments taught: the effect, its uncertainty, and — for observational data — the assumptions it rests on. "Adjusting for prior listening, tenure, Premium status, and device, adopters listen about 4.5 hours more (95% CI 3.6 to 5.3). This estimate assumes that no further differences between adopters and non-adopters affect listening — an assumption that the experiment in Chapter 4, which found 3.2 hours, suggests is not fully met."

The regression toolkit has one more use, which the next chapter develops: it can tell us *for whom* an effect is larger (moderation, through interaction terms like the one in the DiD regression) and *through which mechanism* it works (mediation). That is the subject of @sec-mechanisms.

## Learning check {#sec-lc-05 .unnumbered}

**(LC5.1)** In a regression of listening hours on prior listening hours, the slope is 0.83. Interpret the coefficient in one sentence — and explain why it does not show that listening before the launch *causes* listening after it.

**(LC5.2)** Which statements about adjustment in multiple regression are correct?

- [ ] The coefficient of a variable is its association with the outcome, holding the other variables in the model constant
- [ ] Adding a variable to the model can increase, decrease, or leave unchanged the coefficient of another variable
- [ ] Adjusting for all available variables guarantees an unbiased estimate of a causal effect
- [ ] Adjusting for a mediator removes part of the effect one wants to estimate

**(LC5.3)** A model contains the categorical variable `plan` with the levels "Free", "Premium", and "Family" (reference: Free). The coefficient of `planFamily` is 4.2. Interpret it. How would you test whether the plan matters at all?

**(LC5.4)** A colleague fits a regression with 25 predictors to 300 customers and reports R² = 0.71 for predicting next month's spending. What should you ask before trusting this number?

**(LC5.5)** In a log-log regression, the coefficient of log(advertising spend) is 0.15. (a) Interpret it. (b) The same analysis in levels gives a coefficient of 0.8 sales per euro. Why might the two models reach different conclusions about whether to double the budget?

**(LC5.6)** In a log-level model with the outcome log(sales), the coefficient of a dummy for "promotion week" is 0.35. By what percentage do sales differ in promotion weeks? Use both the approximate and the exact interpretation.

**(LC5.7)** Which statements about logistic regression are correct?

- [ ] It is used when the outcome is a yes/no variable
- [ ] Its coefficients can be read directly as changes in probability
- [ ] Predicted probabilities for different predictor values can be compared to express effects in percentage points
- [ ] It always lies between 0 and 1 in its predictions

**(LC5.8)** An analyst reports a difference-in-differences estimate of a price promotion on sales in treated stores. Which statements are correct?

- [ ] The estimate uses the change in the control stores to estimate what would have happened in the treated stores without the promotion
- [ ] It requires that the treated and control stores had the same sales level before the promotion
- [ ] It requires that both groups would have followed parallel trends without the promotion
- [ ] A placebo test in the pre-period can make the parallel trends assumption more plausible, but cannot prove it

**(LC5.9)** The residual plot of a regression of revenue on advertising shows a funnel: the residuals scatter more widely for large fitted values. What does this mean for the coefficients and for the *p*-values — and what is the simplest fix?

**(LC5.10)** Your group project experiment randomizes two versions of a product description. Afterwards, you also want to know whether the effect differs between frequent and occasional buyers. Which tool from this chapter do you need — and in which chapter is it developed?
